headline: Connecticut fall firearms turkey season opens with updated permission rules
dek: The season runs Oct. 3 through Oct. 31, while a new state rule clarifies when small-game and turkey hunters need landowner permission.
body: Connecticut’s fall firearms turkey season opens Saturday, Oct. 3, and runs through Oct. 31, the Department of Energy and Environmental Protection announced Friday. The opening applies to eligible state and private lands, while the state’s pheasant and broader small-game seasons are scheduled to begin Oct. 17. Fall archery seasons for deer and turkey began Sept. 15, giving Connecticut hunters several overlapping ways to use the state’s forests and private landscapes this month. [DEEP’s opening notice](https://portal.ct.gov/deep/news-releases/news-releases---2026/deep-announces-opening-days-of-fall-turkey-pheasant-and-small-game-hunting-seasons) describes the firearms opener as part of the agency’s annual schedule and urges hunters to participate safely and responsibly.

The basic turkey rules are specific. The fall firearms bag limit is three turkeys of either sex on private land, state land or a combination of the two. Hunting hours begin one-half hour before sunrise and end at sunset. Connecticut residents need a firearms hunting license and a Resident Game Bird Conservation Stamp. Nonresidents need either a three-day out-of-state bird-hunting license or a nonresident firearms license, along with the stamp. The state’s [2026 wild-turkey guide](https://portal.ct.gov/deep/hunting/2026-connecticut-hunting-and-trapping-guide/wild-turkey-hunting) says shotguns must be 20 gauge or larger, use No. 4 through No. 7 1/2 shot or a permitted combination, and be limited to three shells.

Access rules matter as much as the season dates. A hunter on private land must carry signed written consent from the landowner on DEEP’s official form for the current season. Turkey hunting is allowed on Sundays only on private land, and Sunday hunting cannot take place within 40 yards of a blazed public trail. Hunters using state land should check DEEP’s interactive hunting-area map because not every state property is open to fall firearms turkey hunting. Decoys are allowed, but live decoys are prohibited.

The 2026 season also arrives with a permission change that took effect Oct. 1. DEEP says verbal permission is sufficient for small-game hunting on private land every day of the week, including Sundays. Deer and turkey hunters still need written permission from private landowners. The agency also says the legal definition of a muzzleloader has changed: the projectile must be loaded from the muzzle end. Those distinctions are important for people moving between small-game, deer and turkey seasons, because permission requirements do not apply identically to each activity.

DEEP’s safety guidance focuses on preventing a person from being mistaken for a bird. Hunters should remain in a fixed location and call turkeys to them rather than stalk a turkey or a turkey call. Before firing, they should identify the target and what lies beyond it. The guide recommends sitting with protection from an approaching hunter, such as a tree at least as wide as the hunter’s shoulders, and placing a four- to six-inch fluorescent-orange band around the tree about six feet above the ground to identify the calling position. Hunters should not wear red, white, blue or black while turkey hunting, and DEEP recommends fluorescent orange while walking to and from the hunting area and when carrying a harvested bird.

Harvest paperwork continues after a successful hunt. A hunter must immediately complete and sign a Harvest Tag and keep it with the turkey until the carcass is cut up for consumption. DEEP also requires deer and turkey harvests to be reported within 24 hours through its online Hunter Reporting website or by calling 1-877-337-4868, according to the agency’s [fall archery season notice](https://portal.ct.gov/deep/news-releases/news-releases---2026/fall-archery-deer-and-turkey-season-opens-in-september). The reporting requirement gives wildlife managers information for monitoring harvest and managing Connecticut’s turkey population.

For people sharing the woods, the opening changes the mix of activity on public properties beginning this weekend. Hikers and other visitors should pay attention to posted notices and avoid entering closed or restricted areas, while hunters need to confirm the property rules before setting up. DEEP’s guide includes the season dates, license requirements, map links and landowner forms in one place. The next major statewide opening is Oct. 17, when pheasant and several small-game seasons begin; closing dates vary by species.
